items.stem: A question asks you to ‘Identify’ a detail from the passage. What does the examiner expect?
options: A long explanation of the writer’s feelings
A brief, accurate detail taken from the text
An analysis of language
Your own opinion on the topic
items.answer: A brief, accurate detail taken from the text
items.markingKey: ‘Identify’ = pick out; no explanation needed.

items.stem: Question on the review ‘Review: The Floating Museum’: “How many centuries of history does the museum promise to cover?” A student answered: ‘Four centuries’. Using this sentence from the text, explain why the answer is wrong and give the correct answer: “Housed in a converted cargo ship moored in Lisbon’s harbour, the new Museum of the Sea promises ‘an unforgettable voyage through five centuries of ocean history’.”
items.answer: The sentence states that the answer is: Five centuries. The student’s answer is not what the text says (it misreads or confuses the detail).
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: correct answer (Five centuries.); 1 mark: explains that the text states this explicitly and the student’s answer is not supported.

items.stem: Explain why you should check the line or paragraph reference in a retrieval question before answering.
items.answer: The answer must come from the specified part of the text; a similar detail elsewhere may be wrong or not credited.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: answers must be located in the given section; 1 mark: details elsewhere may be different or not accepted. [2]

items.stem: Read this part of the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’ and answer the questions that follow. “It left at nine, after the driver had finished his tea, his second tea and a long conversation with a man selling oranges. Every seat was taken, and the aisle was soon packed with sacks of rice, a crate of hens and a schoolboy who fell asleep standing up.” (a) At what time did the bus actually leave? (b) What was packed into the aisle?
items.answer: (a) Nine o’clock. (b) Sacks of rice, a crate of hens and a sleeping schoolboy.
items.markingKey: (a) Nine o’clock. [1] (b) Sacks of rice, a crate of hens and a sleeping schoolboy. [1]

items.stem: Answer the questions using only this extract from the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’. “Sipho Ndlovu has been called out 212 times in eleven years with the Drakensberg mountain rescue team, and he still keeps his boots by the front door. … Like the rest of the team, he is an unpaid volunteer; by day he teaches mathematics at a local secondary school. … ‘We found them at dawn, cold and frightened but alive. I have never been so tired or so happy.’” (a) When were the two teenagers found? (b) How many times has Sipho been called out, and over how long? (c) What is Sipho’s paid job?
items.answer: (a) At dawn. (b) 212 times in eleven years. (c) He teaches mathematics at a local secondary school.
items.markingKey: (a) At dawn. [1] (b) 212 times in eleven years. [1] (c) He teaches mathematics at a local secondary school. [1]

items.stem: Read this part of the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’ and answer the questions that follow. “It left at nine, after the driver had finished his tea, his second tea and a long conversation with a man selling oranges. Every seat was taken, and the aisle was soon packed with sacks of rice, a crate of hens and a schoolboy who fell asleep standing up. … We arrived eleven hours later, stiff, dusty and somehow friends.” (a) What was packed into the aisle? (b) How long did the journey take? (c) Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘I forgot to be afraid’.
items.answer: (a) Sacks of rice, a crate of hens and a sleeping schoolboy. (b) Eleven hours. (c) For a short time my fear left me.
items.markingKey: (a) Sacks of rice, a crate of hens and a sleeping schoolboy. [1] (b) Eleven hours. [1] (c) For a short time my fear left me; 1 mark for each clear element of the meaning, in own words; repeating the original words gains no credit [2]

items.stem: Read the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’: “Three months after the River Kali burst its banks, recovery in the River District is uneven. Of the 1,400 homes flooded, around 900 have been repaired and reoccupied. The remaining families are still living with relatives or in temporary housing at the sports centre. The main road bridge, which was closed after cracks were found in its supports, reopened last week following emergency repairs costing 2.3 million dollars. However, the district’s only secondary school remains shut, and around 600 students are being taught in shifts at a primary school four kilometres away. Local businesses have been hit hard. A survey by the traders’ association found that one in five shops has not reopened, and many owners say their insurance did not cover flood damage. Engineers have recommended raising the flood wall by one metre and restoring wetlands upstream to slow the water in future. The regional government says it will publish its decision by the end of the year.” Answer the questions. (a) How many flooded homes have been repaired and reoccupied? (b) What proportion of shops has not reopened? (c) Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘burst its banks’.
items.answer: (a) Around 900. (b) One in five. (c) Overflowed and flooded the land around it.
items.markingKey: (a) Around 900. [1] (b) One in five. [1] (c) Overflowed and flooded the land around it; 1 mark for each clear element of the meaning, in own words; repeating the original words gains no credit [2]

items.stem: Read the short story ‘The Night Ferry’: “The ferry left the harbour at nine, an hour late, because the captain refused to cast off until the last delivery van had rattled up the ramp. Mira found a seat on the open deck, her rucksack wedged between her ankles like a nervous dog. Within minutes the lights of the town had shrunk to a smudge, and then the fog swallowed them completely. The engine throbbed beneath her feet. Somewhere below, a child was crying and a radio crackled out a song she half remembered from her grandmother’s kitchen. Mira pulled her scarf tighter. She had told her mother she would be fine travelling alone; she had said it three times, as if repeating it would make it true. Now, with nothing but grey in every direction, she checked her ticket again. Island of Sela, arrival 08:55. Twelve hours. She could manage twelve hours. A deckhand passed, whistling, and nodded at her as though night crossings were the most ordinary thing in the world. For him, she supposed, they were.” Answer the questions. (a) Why did the ferry leave the harbour late? (b) At what time was the ferry due to arrive at the Island of Sela? (c) Where did Mira keep her rucksack during the crossing? (d) What does this suggest about how Mira really felt about travelling alone? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: (a) The captain would not leave until the last delivery van had come on board. (b) 08:55 (c) Wedged between her ankles on the open deck. (d) She was anxious and was trying to convince herself, as well as her mother, that she would be all right. Evidence: ‘she had said it three times’ – repeating the reassurance shows doubt; ‘as if repeating it would make it true’ reveals it did not yet feel true.
items.markingKey: (a) The captain would not leave until the last delivery van had come on board. [1] (b) 08:55 [1] (c) Wedged between her ankles on the open deck. [1] (d) 1 mark: she was anxious and was trying to convince herself, as well as her mother, that she would be all right. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘she had said it three times’ (repeating the reassurance shows doubt; ‘as if repeating it would make it true’ reveals it did not yet feel true) [2]

items.stem: A one-mark question asks ‘When did the ferry leave?’ Which answer is best?
options: In the evening, I think, when it was foggy and Mira was nervous
Late
The ferry left the harbour at nine, an hour late, because the captain refused to cast off until the last van had rattled up the ramp
At nine, an hour late
items.answer: At nine, an hour late
items.markingKey: Precise and relevant.

items.stem: What does it mean to ‘infer’ from a text?
options: To count the number of paragraphs
To work out something that is suggested but not stated directly
To give your own unrelated opinion
To copy the main point word for word
items.answer: To work out something that is suggested but not stated directly
items.markingKey: Inference = reading between the lines using evidence.

items.stem: In the news article ‘Town Votes to Close Main Street to Cars’, the writer writes: ‘Residents of Porto Velho voted on Saturday to close the town’s main street to private cars from next April, ending months of heated debate.’ What does this phrase suggest about the town before the vote? Support your answer with evidence.
items.answer: The issue had divided the town and caused strong, angry disagreement for a long time. Evidence: ‘ending months of heated debate’ – ‘months’ shows length; ‘heated’ shows strong feeling.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: valid inference (the issue had divided the town and caused strong, angry disagreement for a long time.); 1 mark: relevant evidence with explanation (‘months’ shows length; ‘heated’ shows strong feeling). Answers that only retell the text gain no credit.

items.stem: Read this sentence from the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’: ‘A survey by the traders’ association found that one in five shops has not reopened, and many owners say their insurance did not cover flood damage.’ What does this suggest about why some shops have not reopened? Support your answer with evidence.
items.answer: The owners cannot afford the repairs without insurance money. Evidence: ‘many owners say their insurance did not cover flood damage’ – no insurance payout means no money for repairs.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: valid inference (the owners cannot afford the repairs without insurance money.); 1 mark: relevant evidence with explanation (no insurance payout means no money for repairs). Answers that only retell the text gain no credit.

items.stem: The following lines are taken from the news article ‘Town Votes to Close Main Street to Cars’: “Residents of Porto Velho voted on Saturday to close the town’s main street to private cars from next April, ending months of heated debate. … ‘People don’t carry paint tins on a bicycle,’ he said.” What does this comment suggest about Felix Mendes’s attitude to the plan? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: He thinks it is impractical for shops selling heavy goods and will harm his business. Evidence: ‘People don’t carry paint tins on a bicycle’ – the example of heavy paint tins shows customers need cars.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: he thinks it is impractical for shops selling heavy goods and will harm his business. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘People don’t carry paint tins on a bicycle’ (the example of heavy paint tins shows customers need cars) [2]

items.stem: Here is part of the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’: “He pressed his palm flat against the trunk and kept it there. … ‘Plant it somewhere they can’t reach.’” (a) When did Grandfather plant the mango tree? (b) What does this action suggest about Grandfather’s feelings at this moment? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: (a) In the year the narrator’s mother was born. (b) He is grieving and saying a silent goodbye; he wants to stay connected to the tree for as long as he can. Evidence: ‘He pressed his palm flat against the trunk and kept it there.’ – the silence ‘for a long while’ and the lingering touch suggest deep emotion he cannot put into words.
items.markingKey: (a) In the year the narrator’s mother was born. [1] (b) 1 mark: he is grieving and saying a silent goodbye; he wants to stay connected to the tree for as long as he can. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘He pressed his palm flat against the trunk and kept it there.’ (the silence ‘for a long while’ and the lingering touch suggest deep emotion he cannot put into words) [2]

items.stem: The following lines are taken from the diary ‘Turtle Hatchery Diary’: “Last week I mumbled; today they actually asked questions, and one girl wanted to know whether she could volunteer when she is older. … I hope I was telling the truth: the project’s funding ends in December, and nobody knows what happens after that.” (a) How many eggs from Nest 41 did they rescue? (b) What does this suggest about the writer’s feelings about the project’s future? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: (a) Thirty-two. (b) They are worried and uncertain that the project may close and the girl may never be able to volunteer. Evidence: ‘I hope I was telling the truth’ – ‘nobody knows what happens after that’ follows immediately.
items.markingKey: (a) Thirty-two. [1] (b) 1 mark: they are worried and uncertain that the project may close and the girl may never be able to volunteer. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘I hope I was telling the truth’ (‘nobody knows what happens after that’ follows immediately) 1 mark: developed explanation of how the evidence shows this [3]

items.stem: Read this extract from the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’: “He moved slowly between the rows, touching each trunk as if he were taking attendance at a school register. … He pressed his palm flat against the trunk and kept it there. … ‘Plant it somewhere they can’t reach.’” Explain what the writer suggests about the attitudes of the people in this extract. Support each point with evidence and explain how the evidence suggests it.
items.answer: He thinks of them as individuals he is responsible for and cares about, like a teacher with pupils. (‘as if he were taking attendance’: touching ‘each trunk’ shows individual attention and care). He is grieving and saying a silent goodbye; he wants to stay connected to the tree for as long as he can. (‘He pressed his palm flat against the trunk and kept it there.’: the silence ‘for a long while’ and the lingering touch suggest deep emotion he cannot put into words). He resents them and wants something of the orchard to survive beyond their control. (‘Plant it somewhere they can’t reach.’: ‘they’ refers to the developers; ‘can’t reach’ implies they destroy whatever they can get hold of).
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark per valid inference (max 2) and 1 mark per supporting quotation with explanation. Indicative: He thinks of them as individuals he is responsible for and cares about, like a teacher with pupils. (‘as if he were taking attendance’: touching ‘each trunk’ shows individual attention and care). He is grieving and saying a silent goodbye; he wants to stay connected to the tree for as long as he can. (‘He pressed his palm flat against the trunk and kept it there.’: the silence ‘for a long while’ and the lingering touch suggest deep emotion he cannot put into words). He resents them and wants something of the orchard to survive beyond their control. (‘Plant it somewhere they can’t reach.’: ‘they’ refers to the developers; ‘can’t reach’ implies they destroy whatever they can get hold of).

items.stem: Read this extract from the short story ‘First Day at the Workshop’: “‘You’re late,’ he said. … It was enough.” Explain what the writer suggests about the attitudes of the people in this extract. Support each point with evidence and explain how the evidence suggests it.
items.answer: He is testing the narrator, or setting very high, strict standards from the start. (“‘You’re late,’ he said.”: the narrator stays silent and accepts the ‘first lesson’, suggesting it is a deliberate test of attitude). Even this tiny sign of approval makes the narrator feel proud and rewarded for a morning of hard work. (‘It was enough.’: the half-smile is ‘not quite a smile’, yet the narrator values it highly).
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark per valid inference (max 2) and 1 mark per supporting quotation with explanation. Indicative: He is testing the narrator, or setting very high, strict standards from the start. (“‘You’re late,’ he said.”: the narrator stays silent and accepts the ‘first lesson’, suggesting it is a deliberate test of attitude). Even this tiny sign of approval makes the narrator feel proud and rewarded for a morning of hard work. (‘It was enough.’: the half-smile is ‘not quite a smile’, yet the narrator values it highly).

items.stem: Read this sentence from the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’: ‘Sipho Ndlovu has been called out 212 times in eleven years with the Drakensberg mountain rescue team, and he still keeps his boots by the front door.’ What does this detail suggest about Sipho’s commitment? Support your answer with evidence.
items.answer: He is always ready to go and is still fully committed after many years. Evidence: ‘he still keeps his boots by the front door’ – ‘still’ after eleven years and 212 call-outs.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: valid inference (he is always ready to go and is still fully committed after many years.); 1 mark: relevant evidence with explanation (‘still’ after eleven years and 212 call-outs). Answers that only retell the text gain no credit.

items.stem: A question says ‘Using your own words, explain…’. Which answer would gain credit?
options: One that copies the phrase in quotation marks
One that rephrases the meaning without repeating the key words of the text
One that explains how the phrase sounds
One that gives a dictionary page number
items.answer: One that rephrases the meaning without repeating the key words of the text
items.markingKey: Own words = paraphrase; repetition of key words earns nothing.

items.stem: Read this sentence from the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’: ‘Local businesses have been hit hard.’ Using your own words, explain the meaning of ‘hit hard’.
items.answer: Badly affected.
items.markingKey: Mark points: accurate meaning in own words – badly affected. Repeating the key words of the phrase gains no credit.

items.stem: Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘nobody knows what happens after that’ in this sentence from the diary ‘Turtle Hatchery Diary’: ‘I hope I was telling the truth: the project’s funding ends in December, and nobody knows what happens after that.’
items.answer: The future of the project is completely uncertain.
items.markingKey: Mark points: accurate meaning in own words – the future of the project is completely uncertain. Repeating the key words of the phrase gains no credit.

items.stem: Re-read these sentences from the descriptive piece ‘Market Morning’: “Old women haggle with the stallholders as if their lives depended on a few coins, then laugh and pay what was first asked. … By noon the heat presses down like a hand, the shouting softens to murmurs and the traders doze beneath their awnings.” Use your own words in each answer. Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘as if their lives depended on a few coins’.
items.answer: Arguing with great seriousness over a very small amount of money.
items.markingKey: Arguing with great seriousness over a very small amount of money; 1 mark for each clear element of the meaning, in own words; repeating the original words gains no credit [2]

items.stem: Here is part of the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’: “He moved slowly between the rows, touching each trunk as if he were taking attendance at a school register. Most of the trees were already gone; the developers had cleared the eastern field in a single week, and now orange flags fluttered where the guavas had been. … ‘Plant it somewhere they can’t reach.’” Use your own words in each answer. (a) Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘taking attendance at a school register’. (b) Give the meaning of ‘developers’ as it is used in the text.
items.answer: (a) Checking each tree one by one, as a teacher checks that every pupil is present. (b) People or companies who buy land in order to build on it.
items.markingKey: (a) Checking each tree one by one, as a teacher checks that every pupil is present; 1 mark for each clear element of the meaning, in own words; repeating the original words gains no credit [2] (b) People or companies who buy land in order to build on it (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1]

items.stem: In the autobiography ‘Learning to Swim at Forty’, the writer uses the phrase ‘You just have to stop fighting it’. Two students explained it. Student A wrote: ‘It means that You just have to stop fighting it.’ Student B wrote: ‘You need to relax and trust the water instead of struggling against it.’ (a) Using your own words, explain what the writer means by ‘endlessly patient’. (b) Give one piece of advice to Student A for answering ‘own words’ questions. (c) Give the meaning of ‘retired’ as it is used in the text.
items.answer: (a) Never losing her patience, however slow her pupils were. (b) Work out the meaning, then express it with different words (synonyms), keeping the same sense; check no key word from the phrase is repeated. (c) No longer working, usually because of age.
items.markingKey: (a) never losing her patience, however slow her pupils were [2] (b) any sensible, specific advice [1] (c) No longer working, usually because of age (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1]

items.stem: A question is followed by [2] and asks ‘Give two reasons…’. How many separate points should your answer contain?
options: Two
Three
One
As many as possible
items.answer: Two
items.markingKey: One mark per distinct reason.

items.stem: Question on the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’: “What does this suggest about Sipho’s reason for volunteering?” [2] A student answered only by copying: ‘Someone came for my father once, years ago. I suppose I am paying it back.’ Explain why this would not gain both marks, and write an answer that would.
items.answer: Copying the sentence locates the evidence but does not state the inference or explain it. Better: Gratitude: he wants to repay the help his father once received by helping others. This is shown by ‘I suppose I am paying it back’, because ‘Someone came for my father once’.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: copying ≠ explaining the implied meaning; 1 mark: improved answer with inference + evidence (gratitude: he wants to repay the help his father once received by helping others).

items.stem: Question on the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’: “What does this action suggest about the woman beside the writer?” [2] A student answered only by copying: ‘Without a word, she broke a piece from her bread and pressed it into my hand, then pointed out of the window at a line of snow peaks that had appeared above the clouds.’ Explain why this would not gain both marks, and write an answer that would.
items.answer: Copying the sentence locates the evidence but does not state the inference or explain it. Better: She is kind and perceptive; she sees the writer’s fear and offers comfort without fuss. This is shown by ‘Without a word, she broke a piece from her bread’, because ‘The woman beside me noticed’ the white knuckles.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: copying ≠ explaining the implied meaning; 1 mark: improved answer with inference + evidence (she is kind and perceptive; she sees the writer’s fear and offers comfort without fuss).

items.stem: Answer each question about this extract from the diary ‘Turtle Hatchery Diary’, making as many points as the marks indicate. “Ines and I walked the full three kilometres with red torches — white light confuses the turtles — and found two new nests above the tide line. … Last week I mumbled; today they actually asked questions, and one girl wanted to know whether she could volunteer when she is older. … I hope I was telling the truth: the project’s funding ends in December, and nobody knows what happens after that.” What does this suggest about how the writer has changed? Use evidence from the text to support your answer. [2]
items.answer: They have grown in confidence as a speaker since last week. Evidence: ‘Last week I mumbled’ – the contrast between mumbling and the children asking questions shows improvement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: they have grown in confidence as a speaker since last week. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘Last week I mumbled’ (the contrast between mumbling and the children asking questions shows improvement) [2]

items.stem: Answer each question about this extract from the short story ‘Stranded’, making as many points as the marks indicate. “By three o’clock the sky over the ridge had turned the colour of a bruise. … It came over the crest with a howl, snatching Aiko’s hat and flinging it into the valley before either of them could move. … They sat shoulder to shoulder, shaking, and listened to the mountain roar.” (a) What did the wind take from Aiko? [1] (b) What does ‘shoulder to shoulder’ suggest about Kenji and Aiko at the end? Use evidence from the text to support your answer. [2]
items.answer: (a) Her hat. (b) They are close and supporting each other, sharing comfort and relief after the danger. Evidence: ‘They sat shoulder to shoulder’ – physical closeness after shared danger suggests unity and comfort.
items.markingKey: (a) Her hat. [1] (b) 1 mark: they are close and supporting each other, sharing comfort and relief after the danger. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘They sat shoulder to shoulder’ (physical closeness after shared danger suggests unity and comfort) [2]

items.stem: This 3-mark question is about the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’: “Why does the writer say light pollution is ‘not merely a hobby problem’?” [3] Answer A: ‘She expects readers to dismiss her as a stargazer, so she widens the issue to show it affects everyone.’ Answer B: ‘She expects readers to dismiss her as a stargazer, so she widens the issue to show it affects everyone. This is shown when the writer says ‘not merely a hobby problem’, which suggests this because she then lists effects on residents, birds and money.’ (a) Award a mark out of 3 to each answer and justify your decisions. (b) Explain what Answer A needs to do to reach full marks.
items.answer: (a) A: 1/3 – a valid inference but no evidence or explanation. B: 3/3 – inference, apt evidence and developed explanation. (b) Add a short, relevant quotation and explain how it shows the inference.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each for a justified mark for A and B [2] (b) evidence + explanation [2]

items.stem: Which of these is the most common reason for losing marks on retrieval questions?
options: Copying too much text so that the correct detail is buried among wrong details
Using the exact name from the text
Answering in a complete sentence
Writing in pen
items.answer: Copying too much text so that the correct detail is buried among wrong details
items.markingKey: Over-copying can include incorrect material that cancels the answer.

items.stem: Explain why answering a retrieval question in a few precise words can be better than copying a whole sentence.
items.answer: A precise answer shows you have identified exactly what is asked; copying a sentence may include incorrect or irrelevant details that cancel the mark.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: precision shows understanding; 1 mark: over-copying risks contradiction. [2]

items.stem: Read the short story ‘First Day at the Workshop’: “The workshop smelled of pine resin and hot glue, and every surface was furred with sawdust. Mr Okafor did not look up when I came in. He was planing the edge of a door, his whole body leaning into each stroke, and long pale curls of wood spiralled to the floor around his boots. ‘You’re late,’ he said. I was not late; I was ten minutes early. I said nothing. He pointed his chin at a broom propped in the corner, and I understood that this was my first lesson. I swept for an hour. By the time I had finished, my arms ached and the floor gleamed, but he only grunted and handed me a piece of sandpaper and a scrap of rough timber. ‘Smooth,’ he said. ‘Like glass.’ It took me until lunchtime. When he finally ran his thumb along the surface, he paused, and for the briefest moment the corner of his mouth lifted. It was not quite a smile. It was enough.” Answer the questions. (a) How early did the narrator actually arrive? (b) How long did the narrator spend sweeping? (c) What two smells filled the workshop? (d) Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘pointed his chin at a broom’.
items.answer: (a) Ten minutes early. (b) An hour. (c) Pine resin and hot glue. (d) He showed the narrator the broom with a small movement of his head instead of speaking.

He enjoys the danger.
Gratitude: he wants to repay the help his father once received by helping others.

items.stem: Explain the difference between explicit and implicit meaning, using an example of your own.
items.answer: Explicit meaning is stated directly (e.g. ‘She was angry’); implicit meaning is suggested (e.g. ‘She slammed the door’ implies anger).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: explicit = stated; 1 mark: implicit = suggested; 1 mark: apt example. [3]

items.stem: Read this extract from the blog ‘Why I Gave Up My Smartphone for a Month’: “I know because an app told me, which is a bit like a biscuit telling you that you eat too many biscuits. … Honestly, yes; I need it for work.” What does this comparison suggest about the writer’s attitude to the app? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: They find it ironic and slightly absurd that a phone app warned them about using the phone too much. Evidence: ‘which is a bit like a biscuit telling you’ – a biscuit warning about biscuits is self-contradictory.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: they find it ironic and slightly absurd that a phone app warned them about using the phone too much. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘which is a bit like a biscuit telling you’ (a biscuit warning about biscuits is self-contradictory) [2]

items.stem: Read this extract from the leaflet ‘Visiting the Coral Reef Responsibly’: “Help us keep it that way by following these simple guidelines. … It may look like rock, but it is a living animal, and a single touch can damage its delicate outer layer. Use reef-safe sun cream.” Explain what the writer suggests about the thoughts and feelings of the people in this extract. Support each point with evidence and explain how the evidence suggests it.
items.answer: As partners who share responsibility for protecting the reef. (‘Help us keep it that way’: ‘us’ includes visitors in the park’s mission). Visitors may think coral is rock and harmless to touch, so the writers correct this to make them take care. (‘It may look like rock, but it is a living animal’: ‘may look like rock, but’ corrects a likely misunderstanding).
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark per valid inference (max 2) and 1 mark per supporting quotation with explanation. Indicative: As partners who share responsibility for protecting the reef. (‘Help us keep it that way’: ‘us’ includes visitors in the park’s mission). Visitors may think coral is rock and harmless to touch, so the writers correct this to make them take care. (‘It may look like rock, but it is a living animal’: ‘may look like rock, but’ corrects a likely misunderstanding).

items.stem: Question on the report ‘Canteen Food Waste Report’: “What does the Friday finding suggest about the cause of waste on that day?” [2] A student answered only by copying: ‘Waste was highest on Fridays, when a quarter of students said they skipped lunch to leave early for sports fixtures.’ Explain why this would not gain both marks, and write an answer that would.
items.answer: Copying the sentence locates the evidence but does not state the inference or explain it. Better: Food is cooked for more students than actually eat, because many leave early for sport. This is shown by ‘a quarter of students said they skipped lunch’, because waste is highest when fewer students eat.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: copying ≠ explaining the implied meaning; 1 mark: improved answer with inference + evidence (food is cooked for more students than actually eat, because many leave early for sport).

items.stem: Explicit information is
options: only found in the title
stated directly in the text
hinted at but never stated
the reader’s own opinion
items.answer: stated directly in the text
items.markingKey: Explicit = stated; implicit = suggested.

items.stem: Question on the memoir ‘My Grandmother’s Kitchen’: “In which city was the grandmother’s kitchen?” A student answered: ‘Accra’. Using this sentence from the text, explain why the answer is wrong and give the correct answer: ‘My grandmother’s kitchen in Lagos was never quiet.’
items.answer: The sentence states that the answer is: Lagos. The student’s answer is not what the text says (it misreads or confuses the detail).
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: correct answer (Lagos.); 1 mark: explains that the text states this explicitly and the student’s answer is not supported.

(b) How many times a day did the writer use to check the phone?
items.answer: (a) About forty minutes more a night. (b) 140 times.
items.markingKey: (a) About forty minutes more a night. [1] (b) 140 times. [1]

items.stem: Read the blog ‘Street Food Fridays’: “Every Friday at six, the car park behind Colombo’s old railway station turns into the best restaurant in the city. No tables, no menus, no reservations — just thirty-odd stalls, a few strings of coloured bulbs and a crowd that grows until you can barely move. My first stop is always Ravi’s kottu stall, where two flat-topped grills clatter like a drum band as he chops roti, egg and vegetables together with a pair of steel blades. A plate costs less than a bus ticket. Next, I queue for hoppers: crisp, bowl-shaped pancakes with a soft egg at the centre. I have burned my fingers on them every single week and I regret nothing. Not everything is perfect. There are not enough bins, and by nine the ground is littered with paper plates. But the council has promised more bins from next month, and the traders now run a tidy-up rota. Come hungry, bring cash, and wear shoes you don’t mind ruining.” Answer the questions. (a) About how many stalls are there? (b) What has the council promised? (c) What does this suggest about the writer’s feelings about hoppers? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: (a) About thirty. (b) More bins from next month. (c) They love them so much that the pain is worth it; it shows enthusiasm and humour. Evidence: ‘I have burned my fingers on them every single week and I regret nothing’ – ‘I regret nothing’ shows the pleasure outweighs the pain.
items.markingKey: (a) About thirty. [1] (b) More bins from next month. [1] (c) 1 mark: they love them so much that the pain is worth it; it shows enthusiasm and humour. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘I have burned my fingers on them every single week and I regret nothing’ (‘I regret nothing’ shows the pleasure outweighs the pain) [2]

items.stem: Read the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’: “Sipho Ndlovu has been called out 212 times in eleven years with the Drakensberg mountain rescue team, and he still keeps his boots by the front door. ‘The phone can ring at three in the morning,’ he says. ‘You have perhaps ten minutes to be in the truck.’ Like the rest of the team, he is an unpaid volunteer; by day he teaches mathematics at a local secondary school. Most call-outs, he explains, are not dramatic falls but simple mistakes: hikers who set off too late, who underestimate how quickly the weather changes, or who rely on a phone battery that dies on the mountain. The worst night he remembers was a search for two teenagers in thick cloud. ‘We found them at dawn, cold and frightened but alive. I have never been so tired or so happy.’ Asked why he continues, he shrugs. ‘Someone came for my father once, years ago. I suppose I am paying it back.’” Answer the questions. (a) How long do volunteers have to reach the truck after a call? (b) What is Sipho’s paid job? (c) When were the two teenagers found? (d) Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘paying it back’.
items.answer: (a) About ten minutes. (b) He teaches mathematics at a local secondary school. (c) At dawn. (d) Repaying a kindness by helping others in turn.
items.markingKey: (a) About ten minutes. [1] (b) He teaches mathematics at a local secondary school. [1] (c) At dawn. [1] (d) Repaying a kindness by helping others in turn; 1 mark for each clear element of the meaning, in own words; repeating the original words gains no credit [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) What does it mean to ‘infer’ from a text? (b) A strong inference answer should
items.answer: (a) To work out something that is suggested but not stated directly (b) state the implied meaning and support it with evidence from the text
items.markingKey: (a) Inference = reading between the lines using evidence. (b) Point + evidence + explanation.

items.stem: Explain why an inference must be supported by evidence from the text.
items.answer: Without evidence, the answer is just a guess or personal opinion; evidence shows the inference is grounded in what the writer has written.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inference must be grounded; 1 mark: evidence shows how the meaning is suggested. [2]

items.stem: Read this extract from the short story ‘The Audition’: “The corridor outside Room 4 was lined with plastic chairs, and on every chair sat someone more talented than Tomás. … Tomás closed his eyes and pictured the kitchen at home, the grey light at six o’clock, his mother pretending to sleep through his scales. When the man returned and said ‘Tomás Ferreira?’, he was surprised to find that his hands had stopped shaking.” Explain what the writer suggests about the thoughts and feelings of the people in this extract. Support each point with evidence and explain how the evidence suggests it.
items.answer: He lacks confidence and compares himself unfavourably with everyone else. (‘on every chair sat someone more talented than Tomás’: ‘At least, that was how it felt’ shows this is his fear, not a fact). She is patient and supportive; she puts up with the early-morning noise to encourage him. (‘his mother pretending to sleep through his scales’: ‘pretending’ shows she is awake but chooses not to complain).

She is patient and supportive; she puts up with the early-morning noise to encourage him. (‘his mother pretending to sleep through his scales’: ‘pretending’ shows she is awake but chooses not to complain).

items.stem: Question on the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’: “Why does the writer include this sentence?” [2] A student answered only by copying: ‘I am not arguing for banning homework altogether.’ Explain why this would not gain both marks, and write an answer that would.
items.answer: Copying the sentence locates the evidence but does not state the inference or explain it. This is shown by ‘I am not arguing for banning homework altogether’, because it is a concession before the main proposal.

items.stem: Answer each question about this extract from the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’, making as many points as the marks indicate. “Light pollution is not merely a hobby problem for people like me. … A simple solution exists: motion-sensor lighting, which switches on only when someone is present.” (a) What solution does the writer propose? [1] (b) Why does the writer say light pollution is ‘not merely a hobby problem’? Use evidence from the text to support your answer. [2]
items.answer: (a) Motion-sensor lighting that switches on only when someone is present. (b) She expects readers to dismiss her as a stargazer, so she widens the issue to show it affects everyone. Evidence: ‘not merely a hobby problem’ – she then lists effects on residents, birds and money.
